title: Degrees of comparison of adverbs
shortExplanation: faster, more carefully, best, worse, further
longExplanation:
Adverbs form degrees of comparison according to the same rules as adjectives.
• Monosyllabic: + er/est: fast→faster, hard→harder, early→earlier
• Most on -ly: more/most: carefully→more carefully→most carefully
• Incorrect: well→better→best, badly→worse→worst, far→further→furthest, little→less→least, much→more→most
formation: faster, more carefully, best, worse, further

examples.sentence: She spoke more confidently than before.
examples.translation: She spoke more confidently than before.

examples.sentence: He works hardest in the team.
examples.translation: He works harder than anyone on the team.

title: Inversion with negative adverbs
shortExplanation: Never have I seen this. Rarely does she complain.
longExplanation:
For emphasis, the negative adverb/expression is placed at the beginning → auxiliary verb before the subject (word order as in a question).
Words that trigger inversion: never, rarely, rarely, little, hardly, scarcely, barely, not only, only, no sooner
formation: Never have I seen this. Rarely does she complain.

examples.sentence: Never have I seen anything so beautiful.
examples.translation: I have never seen anything so beautiful.

examples.sentence: Rarely does she make a mistake.
examples.translation: She rarely makes mistakes.

examples.sentence: Little did I know what was coming.
examples.translation: I had no idea what was waiting for me.

pattern: Not only... but also with inversion
title: Not only... but also with inversion
shortExplanation: Not only did he apologise, but he also offered to help.
longExplanation:
Not only + inversion in the first part, the second part is the usual order.
Used for emphasis: expresses that something went further than expected.
formation: Not only did he apologise, but he also offered to help.

examples.sentence: Not only is she talented, but she is also very hard-working.
examples.translation: She is not only talented, but also very hardworking.

examples.sentence: Not only did they arrive late, but they also forgot the documents.
examples.translation: They were not only late, but also forgot their documents.

title: Hardly / Scarcely / No sooner + inversion
shortExplanation: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.
longExplanation:
Immediate sequence constructions:
• Hardly/Scarcely + had + subject + V3 + when/before + Past Simple
• No sooner + had + subject + V3 + than + Past Simple
formation: Hardly had I sat down when the phone rang.

examples.sentence: Hardly had she arrived when it started to rain.
examples.translation: She had barely arrived when it started to rain.

examples.sentence: No sooner had I sat down than someone knocked at the door.
examples.translation: I had just sat down when someone knocked on the door.

title: Inversion in conditionals: Had / Were / Should
shortExplanation: Had I known (= If I had known). Were I you (= If I were you).
longExplanation:
Formal style - excludes if, uses inversion:
• Had + subject + V3 = If + Past Perfect (3rd type)
• Were + subject (+ to + infinitive) = If + Past Simple (2nd type)
• Should + subject + infinitive = If (unlikely, type 1)
formation: Had I known (= If I had known). Were I you (= If I were you).

examples.sentence: Had she told me, I would have helped.
examples.translation: If she had told me, I would have helped.

examples.sentence: Were I in your position, I would accept.
examples.translation: If I were you, I would agree.

examples.sentence: Should you need assistance, please call us.
examples.translation: If you need assistance, call us.

title: It-cleft: It was John who called.
shortExplanation: To highlight any member of a sentence
longExplanation:
Structure: It + to be + selected element + who/that/which + rest
Shifts the focus of attention to the highlighted element.
• For people - who; for things/circumstances - that/which.
formation: To highlight any member of a sentence

examples.sentence: It was the noise that woke me up. (не шум вообще, именно этот)
examples.translation: It was the noise that woke me up.

examples.sentence: It is hard work that leads to success.
examples.translation: It is hard work that leads to success.

title: Wh-cleft: What surprised me was the price.
shortExplanation: What I need is rest. What she said shocked everyone.
longExplanation:
Structure: What + subordinate clause + to be + highlighted element
Emphasizes the importance of the element introduced at the end.
formation: What I need is rest. What she said shocked everyone.

examples.sentence: What I love about London is the diversity.
examples.translation: What I like most about London is the diversity.

examples.sentence: What he did was completely unexpected.
examples.translation: What he did was completely unexpected.

pattern: Formal subjunctive after verbs of demand
title: Formal subjunctive after verbs of demand
shortExplanation: I suggest he leave. It is vital that she be informed.
longExplanation:
After suggest, recommend, insist, demand, propose, request, require, ask, advise, order + that - the basic form of the verb for all persons (without -s, without was).
The British version often uses should instead of the subjunctive: I suggest that he should leave.
American - often a pure subjunctive.
formation: I suggest he leave. It is vital that she be informed.

examples.sentence: I recommend that he see a doctor.
examples.translation: I recommend that he see a doctor.

examples.sentence: It is essential that all students attend the meeting.
examples.translation: It is essential that all students attend the meeting.

title: It's high time + Past Simple
shortExplanation: It's high time you went to bed. It's time we left.
longExplanation:
It's (high/about) time + subject + Past Simple
Meaning: present/future - we are talking about something that should have been done a long time ago.
high time - even stronger: it’s high time!
formation: It's high time you went to bed. It's time we left.

examples.sentence: It's time she found a new job.
examples.translation: It's high time she found a new job.

examples.sentence: It's high time you apologised.
examples.translation: It's high time to apologize.

title: as if / as though + subjunctive
shortExplanation: She talks as if she knew everything. He looked as though he had seen a ghost.
longExplanation:
as if / as though + Past Simple is an unrealistic comparison in the present.
as if / as though + Past Perfect is an unrealistic comparison about the past.
formation: She talks as if she knew everything. He looked as though he had seen a ghost.

examples.sentence: He spends money as if he were a millionaire.
examples.translation: He spends money like he's a millionaire.

examples.sentence: She spoke as though she had met him before.
examples.translation: She spoke as if she had met him before.

title: So / Neither + auxiliary verb + subject
shortExplanation: So do I. Neither does she. So am I.
longExplanation:
So + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the affirmative.
Neither/Nor + auxiliary + subject - agreement with the negative.
The auxiliary verb must coincide with the tense of the original sentence.
formation: So do I. Neither does she. So am I.

examples.sentence: I love jazz. So does she.
examples.translation: I love jazz. She too.

examples.sentence: I haven't been to Rome. Neither have I.
examples.translation: I haven't been to Rome. Me too.

pattern: I think so / I hope so / I'm afraid so
title: I think so / I hope so / I'm afraid so
shortExplanation: Will it rain? - I think so. / I hope not.
longExplanation:
so replaces the subordinate clause after: think, hope, suppose, expect, believe, imagine, be afraid.
Negative form: not (not so not!).
formation: Will it rain? - I think so. / I hope not.

examples.sentence: Will he come? — I think so. / I don't think so.
examples.translation: Will he come? - I think yes. / Don't think.

examples.sentence: Is it expensive? — I'm afraid so.
examples.translation: Is it expensive? - I'm afraid so.

examples.sentence: Is it closed? — I hope not.
examples.translation: Closed? - I hope not.

title: Inclusive vs non-inclusive clauses
shortExplanation: The man who called is my brother. VS My brother, who called, is a doctor.
longExplanation:
Defining: specifies who/what we are talking about - without commas. that is possible. The pronoun can be omitted if it is an object.
Non-defining: adds information - commas required. Only who/which (not that!). The pronoun cannot be omitted.
formation: The man who called is my brother. VS My brother, who called, is a doctor.

examples.sentence: The film that won the Oscar was brilliant. (определяет, о каком фильме речь)
examples.translation: The film that won the Oscar was great.

examples.sentence: Avatar, which came out in 2009, was a huge hit. (доп. факт о и так известном фильме)
examples.translation: Avatar, released in 2009, became a big hit.

title: Preposition + which/whom in formal style
shortExplanation: The company for which I work. The person with whom I spoke.
longExplanation:
Formal style: preposition + which/whom before a relative pronoun.
Informal equivalent: preposition at the end of a sentence.
whom is the formal object form of who.
formation: The company for which I work. The person with whom I spoke.

examples.sentence: The report to which I referred is attached. (формально)
examples.translation: The report I mentioned is attached.

examples.sentence: The report which I referred to is attached. (нейтрально)
The report I referred to is attached. (разговорно)

title: Nominalization - Basics
longExplanation:
Nominalization is the conversion of verbs/adjectives into nouns. A sign of academic and business style.
Main suffixes:
• -tion/-sion: decide→decision, discuss→discussion
• -ment: improve→improvement, develop→development
• -ance/-ence: appear→appearance, differ→difference
• -ity: complex→complexity, able→ability
• -ness: happy→happiness, aware→awareness

examples.sentence: She decided to expand. → Our decision to expand the company...
examples.translation: Our decision to expand...

examples.sentence: He discovered that... → His discovery of the error...
examples.translation: His discovery of the error...
